content: The long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (LCPUFAs), specifically docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) and arachidonic acid (AA), are critical for the development and maturation of the brain, retina, and other organs in newborn infants. Standard infant formulas do not include LCPUFAs; instead, they contain alpha-linolenic acid and linoleic acid, which must be converted by formula-fed infants into DHA and AA. Recently, some manufacturers have started adding LCPUFAs to infant formulas, promoting these products as beneficial for the overall development of full-term infants. The objective of this study was to evaluate whether supplementing formula milk with LCPUFAs is both safe and advantageous for full-term infants, with a focus on its effects on visual function, neurodevelopment, and physical growth. To achieve this, a systematic review of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) was conducted. The search included databases such as CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and CINAHL, covering studies up to December 2016. Only RCTs that assessed the effects of LCPUFA-supplemented versus non-supplemented formula on visual, neurodevelopmental, and growth outcomes were included. Trials that reported only biochemical outcomes were excluded. A total of 31 RCTs were identified, of which 15 studies involving 1,889 infants were included in the review. Nine studies assessed visual acuity, with six using visual evoked potentials (VEP), two using Teller cards, and one using both methods. Four studies reported beneficial effects of LCPUFA supplementation on visual acuity, while five did not. A meta-analysis of three RCTs demonstrated a significant improvement in sweep VEP acuity at 12 months (mean difference (MD) -0.15 logMAR, 95% confidence interval (CI) -0.17 to -0.13; N = 244). However, another meta-analysis of three RCTs found no benefit for visual acuity measured with Teller cards at 12 months (MD -0.01 cycles/degree, 95% CI -0.12 to 0.11; N = 256). The overall quality of evidence for visual acuity outcomes, as assessed by GRADE, was low. Neurodevelopmental outcomes were evaluated in 11 studies, with nine using the Bayley Scales of Infant Development, version II (BSID-II). Only two studies reported beneficial effects. Meta-analyses revealed no significant differences between LCPUFA-supplemented and placebo groups in BSID Mental Developmental Index (MDI) scores at 18 months (MD 0.06, 95% CI -2.01 to 2.14; N = 661) or in BSID Psychomotor Development Index (PDI) scores at 18 months (MD 0.69, 95% CI -0.78 to 2.16; N = 661). Similarly, no significant differences were observed in BSID-II scores at one or two years of age. One study reported improved novelty preference at nine months using the Fagan Infant Test, and another reported better problem-solving abilities at 10 months. However, a study using the Brunet and Lezine test found no benefits. Long-term follow-up of some infants at three, six, and nine years of age also showed no advantages of supplementation. The overall quality of evidence for neurodevelopmental outcomes was rated as low. Thirteen studies assessed physical growth, and none reported either beneficial or harmful effects of LCPUFA supplementation. A meta-analysis of five RCTs found that the supplemented group had lower weight z-scores at one year of age (MD -0.23, 95% CI -0.40 to -0.06; N = 521). However, no significant differences were observed between the groups in terms of length or head circumference z-scores. Meta-analyses at 18 months and two years of age showed no significant differences in weight (kg), length (cm), or head circumference (cm) between the two groups. The overall quality of evidence for growth outcomes was also low. In conclusion, the majority of the included RCTs did not demonstrate consistent beneficial effects or harms of LCPUFA supplementation on the neurodevelopmental outcomes of formula-fed full-term infants. Similarly, no consistent benefits were observed for visual acuity or physical growth. Based on the current evidence, routine supplementation of full-term infant formula with LCPUFAs cannot be recommended.
